Theory

A gut feeling. Credible, often hard-won, sometimes obviously true — but nobody has yet quantified the cause and effect behind it. Practitioner wisdom lives here until it is measured, which is not a demotion: it is an admission that we have not done the work.

ideation · 101

Theory ideation · earlier check spanned 46 channels
A format is only real if you can list 20 viable episodes before launching it; a variable space that yields three inputs is a mini-series, not a franchise.
Source: idea-engine research dossier
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — which is exactly why it sits at Theory rather than higher — the rung means the cause and effect behind it has not been quantified. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Realized breadth buys nothing measurable: Spearman(evidence count, reported lift) = -0.15 across 57 formats, and 16 formats post >=2x median lift on only 2-7 realized instances. The widest runs we hold sit at or below channel-normal — ISHITANI 'Making <Piece>' 1.20-1.32x over 24, Channel C's store run 1.03x over 20, Channel A's game frame 1.00x over 14, Motovudu's Q&A 0.74x over 11.

Caveat: Episodes MADE is not episodes LISTABLE, and the claim is a screening rule applied before launch — a format could pass the 20-episode test and then be run only 4 times. What our data can say is that a large realized episode count is not itself a marker of a strong format, which is a weaker statement than the claim makes and does not refute it.

Where the claim came from
Before declaring a format, list 20 viable episodes. The list is not a publishing commitment; it reveals whether the variable space is rich enough and whether the production system can sustain the promise.

Before adopting a format found in outlier research, test its REPEATABILITY: if you cannot name seven or eight topic variations that fit the same sentence structure, reject the idea even though it is a genuine outlier.
Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Repeatability does not predict lift in our library: Spearman(evidence count, lift) = -0.15 across 57 formats; the highest-lift shapes are the thinnest. Meanwhile the payoff the rule is protecting — that a repeatable format's later instances reproduce the first — does not materialise: repeats of a >=1.5x instance return median 1.01x with 0 of 9 reaching 1.5x, and only 33% of repeats after ANY >=1.5x instance beat 1.5x against a 20% base rate (25 channels, n=64).

Caveat: Nameable variations are not observable in our data, so this tests a proxy. The result cuts an awkward way: the screen may still be worth applying for production-planning reasons, but our evidence says passing it does not predict that instance two will work.

Formats work as a 'roulette wheel': a fixed clause ('I survived…', 'Overnight at…', 'I survived on a penny') plus a rotating variable, so half the title is already solved and ideation reduces to enumerating plug-in subjects — which means ideas can come from effort rather than creativity.
Source: Ryan Trahan

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The 'pure repetition underperforms' premise is supported: repeated-signature videos run 0.954x age-adjusted vs 1.016x for unique ones (33 channels, p=0.0076), and repeats of a proven >=1.5x instance land at median 1.01x with 0 of 9 reaching 1.5x again. The 'pure novelty underperforms' premise is NOT supported — unique-signature videos are the better-performing group in our data, not a penalised one. The 3:1 ratio itself is unmeasurable here.

Caveat: A within-channel normalised score cannot rank channels against each other, so no slate-mix claim of this shape is testable with the data we hold. Testing it properly needs channel-level growth outcomes over time against a measured repeat/new ratio, which we could build from repeated crawls but do not have yet.

Where the claim came from
Can you see there's a good ratio? The ratio I recommend is something between three double downs and one innovative idea.
Theory ideation · earlier check spanned 32 channels
An audience's liking for a creative element follows an inverted-U against exposure count: it rises with repetition to a peak, then every further exposure reduces liking — so a format has a finite number of uses before it starts costing performance.
Source: Alan Garnett

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: No rise phase appears anywhere. Raw instalment medians fall monotonically (1.39 / 1.12 / 1.00 / 0.70) and age-adjusted they are flat (1.08 / 1.02 / 0.88 / 0.84). Channel C's 20-instalment run: first-5 median 0.90x, last-5 median 0.94x — no peak. Motovudu's 11 parts sit in a 0.61-1.10 band with the highest values at parts 15-19, which is a late rise if anything. Channel A's 14-instalment frame trends slightly upward (+0.14).

Caveat: We measure views and retention, not liking, and the claim is about an affective response. Our runs may all sit on one side of a peak we cannot see. Treat this as 'the predicted shape is not visible in performance data', not as a refutation of the psychology.

Where the claim came from
The students enjoyment of the music followed a bell shaped curve from the second to the eighth time they were exposed to each song.
Theory ideation · earlier check spanned 10 channels
Review and product/tool spotlight formats win clickability but lose replayability: they produce the channel's highest CTR and views while producing its LOWEST new-viewer-return rate and lowest APV — they buy an audience that does not come back.
Source: our own channel audits
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What is this channel's binding constraint — ACQUISITION or RETURN — and is the reviewed OBJECT the subscription proposition or is the creator? A gear channel whose viewers subscribe to hear about the next product is not harmed by object-led loyalty; a personality channel using reviews as filler is trading its return rate for upload cadence. The complementary format finding is already in the store (11d4f227f7ea): serialised formats invert the pattern exactly — highest return rate and highest AVD, no new-viewer acquisition — which means the two are a portfolio pair, not competing recommendations. Our corpus confirms the clickability half at scale in one niche: review-shaped patterns dominate the motorcycle format table (Motorcycle CarPlay Product Review 2.61x n=7, Provocative Take + Bike Review 2.29x n=3, Product Full Review 1.67x n=16). We hold no return-rate or subscriber-conversion data, so the cost half stays untested here.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Views half is a null: WITH n=105 median 1.04x vs 1.00x (MWU z=0.77, p=0.44); age-adjusted identical at 1.04x vs 1.00x (p=0.43). Channels split 7 ahead / 3 behind, and the spread is wide — FortNine 1.19x vs 0.59x and John Malecki 1.60x vs 0.90x against RevZilla 0.66x vs 3.17x and TheMissendenFlyer 0.82x vs 1.03x. Retention half matches the claim's direction but on almost no data: our 3 review videos retain 22.2% at half against 35.7% for the other 116; Channel D alone shows the exact predicted pattern — reviews 19% retention at 1.20x views vs 28% retention at 0.95x views for the rest.

Caveat: The claim's two strongest components (CTR, new-viewer return) are untestable here, so a verdict on the whole claim is not available. The retention evidence is 3 videos on 1 channel — an anecdote. The views half is genuinely null across 10 channels, which at least contradicts 'highest views of any format'.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Points mildly the OTHER way: WITH n=26 median 0.84x vs 1.00x (MWU z=-1.71, p=0.087); age-adjusted 0.94x vs 1.00x (z=-0.82, p=0.41). Only 2 of the 5 channels with >=2 matching videos came out ahead (FortNine 1.58x vs 1.00x, a peer channel 1.08x vs 1.00x) against three behind. Channel A's 'Surviving 50 Nights at GRANDMAS' returned 1.65x while 'Roblox SIT OR DIE' returned 0.69x, so the keyword does not separate outcomes on our own channels either.

Caveat: Implied danger is a property of the PREMISE, and title keywords catch it badly — a gaming channel's 'die' is not physical risk, and a genuinely dangerous stunt can be titled blandly. The age-adjusted result is a clean null rather than a reversal. I would not report this as refuting the claim; it refutes only the idea that danger words in a title are a reliable lever.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Retention half points the claimed way: repeated-signature videos on our channels retain 39.7% at half vs 35.0% for unique-signature videos (n=18 vs 101, MWU z=2.09, p=0.037). But those videos are also SHORTER — median 19.9 min vs 24.2 min — and Spearman(duration, retention at 50%) = -0.29 across the same 119 videos, so the retention edge is plausibly a length artifact rather than a serialisation effect. Views half is consistent with 'no acquisition': numbered-series videos in the corpus run 0.87x vs 1.00x raw (n=81, p=0.055) and 0 of the 4 channels with >=2 series videos had them ahead (Motovudu 0.74x vs 1.75x, Yammie Noob 0.54x vs 1.27x, John Heisz 0.68x vs 1.13x, Moto Camp Nerd 0.43x vs 1.08x); age-adjusted the pooled gap vanishes (0.99x vs 1.00x).

Caveat: The load-bearing half of the claim — return rate — is untestable with our data. The retention result is confounded by duration and rests on 18 videos across 4 channels using a crude signature proxy for 'serialised'. The views result survives raw but not age adjustment, so it is not safe to lean on either.

Where the claim came from
Overall, Series are GREAT for Watchability, Need to increase new viewer appeal

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Series markers (Part N / Ep N / #N / Day N) run 0.87x vs 1.00x raw across 46 channels (n=81, p=0.055) and were behind in all 4 channels with >=2 such videos, though the gap disappears once age is controlled (0.99x vs 1.00x). Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: No support at the title level: WITH n=20 median 0.85x vs 1.00x (MWU z=-1.51, p=0.13); age-adjusted 0.93x vs 1.00x (z=-1.08, p=0.28). Only 1 of 3 channels with >=2 matching videos came out ahead (Stuff Made Here 1.29x vs 0.99x; William Osman 0.50x vs 1.06x; PrestonGamez 0.70x vs 1.09x). A money-contrast proxy fares no better: '$' in title returns 1.04x vs 1.00x (p=0.53) across 46 channels.

Caveat: 'vs' is a narrow proxy for a broad mechanism — the claim's own examples ('Luxurious Prisons', a Simpsons episode about depression) contain no versus construction at all, so most genuine contrast ideas are invisible to this test. The claim is also comparative ('most reusable'), which would require ranking mechanisms we cannot each isolate. This is a null on one narrow operationalisation, not a refutation.

Where the claim came from
This is the most common one used by a lot of creators where you contrast two things. Simon, $20,000 versus $200 hotel. You're contrasting a very expensive and cheap hotel. Luxurious prisons. A prison is not supposed to be luxurious.
Theory ideation
An outlier that the creator's OWN viewers are also watching is a materially stronger signal than an equally high-performing outlier from a merely similar channel — but neither establishes causation.
Source: idea-engine research dossier

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which layer are you generating at — a NEW FORMAT or a NEW EPISODE inside a proven one? Fixation is a risk only where the output is supposed to be structurally novel; where the output is deliberately a variant of a known structure, exposure is not contamination, it is the input. The operationally useful split: run the anti-fixation freeze at the format/premise layer, and run outlier study at the topic/variable layer — which is precisely Marcus Jones's own asymmetry (topics inside, formats outside) read one level up. Erik Bork (02de88eed921) marks the third position: once you have generated, WATCH the competitor's version rather than avoiding it, because the differences are what make yours viable. So the rule is sequenced, not opposed — the store currently holds three timestamps of one process as three competing doctrines.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the constraint INVISIBLE (a production limit that shapes what gets made — budget, crew, shooting days) or PACKAGED (a rule stated in the title that the viewer must accept before clicking)? The evidence divides cleanly on that line and on nothing else: every pro-constraint claim is about production, and every anti-constraint claim is about a constraint the audience can see. An invisible constraint costs the creator options and buys focus; a packaged constraint costs total addressable market and buys a promise. The dossier's own twist rule (e8765927f618) is the test for the second kind — a constraint earns its place only when it alters the decision, difficulty, evidence or payoff, and destroys the format when it is invisible, cheatable, or so tight the outcome is predetermined.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does this channel's demand arrive PULLED (a viewer types a query — how-to, product research, education, urgent repair) or PUSHED (browse and suggested)? Cannell's claim is already tagged to education and Galloway's already excludes search-driven channels, so the two rules are compatible the moment neither is stated as universal — but Eves's is stated universally, and that is the repair the store needs. Our corpus offers indirect support for the split: the search-driven motorcycle niche is the one where long titles help (+0.07 at n=127) and where naming a specific machine produced 12.0% CTR against a 4.40% channel average (7470d720ee0b), while browse-driven roblox punishes long titles hard (0.72x, -0.28). Add a required trafficSource scope tag to every packaging claim; roughly a third of this slice is silently conditioned on it.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the gate apply to the SUBJECT or to the FRAME? Thomas Brag's 'hide the vegetables' case (0f3a8d1320d9) is the resolution sitting unused in the store: the same Moldova footage failed as 'Spending a Day with a Grandpa in Eastern Europe' and worked as 'Traveling to the Worst Country in Europe'. The subject was unpackageable; a frame existed. So the defensible rule is 'kill an idea for which no FRAME can be found', not 'kill a mundane subject' — and the correct funnel step is a frame-search pass before the kill, which none of the five gate statements includes. The second discriminator is traffic source: the gate is a browse-competition rule, and a channel whose views arrive from an established subscriber relationship (Brag's own 417a2ab32d77 — no objectively great idea, only ideas great for a channel at a stage) faces a much weaker version of it.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is creator feeling being used as a VETO or as a SELECTOR? The bias Gannett identifies runs in one direction — saturation exposure makes creators crave more novelty than their audience does, corroborated by Erik Bork twice over (1b71420b9852: inexperienced work over-indexes on being different and fails on the other six criteria; 0bb10fcb4588: audiences value newness less than creators and critics do, preferring a known type with one big new thing). So boredom is diagnostic and excitement is not: 'this bores me' is trustworthy because a predictable ending for the maker is a predictable ending for the audience, while 'this excites me' is exactly where the saturation bias lives. Scope the two claims as a veto rule and a selection prohibition and both survive intact.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the constraint INVISIBLE (a production limit that shapes what gets made — budget, crew, shooting days) or PACKAGED (a rule stated in the title that the viewer must accept before clicking)? The evidence divides cleanly on that line and on nothing else: every pro-constraint claim is about production, and every anti-constraint claim is about a constraint the audience can see. An invisible constraint costs the creator options and buys focus; a packaged constraint costs total addressable market and buys a promise. The dossier's own twist rule (e8765927f618) is the test for the second kind — a constraint earns its place only when it alters the decision, difficulty, evidence or payoff, and destroys the format when it is invisible, cheatable, or so tight the outcome is predetermined.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which layer are you generating at — a NEW FORMAT or a NEW EPISODE inside a proven one? Fixation is a risk only where the output is supposed to be structurally novel; where the output is deliberately a variant of a known structure, exposure is not contamination, it is the input. The operationally useful split: run the anti-fixation freeze at the format/premise layer, and run outlier study at the topic/variable layer — which is precisely Marcus Jones's own asymmetry (topics inside, formats outside) read one level up. Erik Bork (02de88eed921) marks the third position: once you have generated, WATCH the competitor's version rather than avoiding it, because the differences are what make yours viable. So the rule is sequenced, not opposed — the store currently holds three timestamps of one process as three competing doctrines.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the gate apply to the SUBJECT or to the FRAME? Thomas Brag's 'hide the vegetables' case (0f3a8d1320d9) is the resolution sitting unused in the store: the same Moldova footage failed as 'Spending a Day with a Grandpa in Eastern Europe' and worked as 'Traveling to the Worst Country in Europe'. The subject was unpackageable; a frame existed. So the defensible rule is 'kill an idea for which no FRAME can be found', not 'kill a mundane subject' — and the correct funnel step is a frame-search pass before the kill, which none of the five gate statements includes. The second discriminator is traffic source: the gate is a browse-competition rule, and a channel whose views arrive from an established subscriber relationship (Brag's own 417a2ab32d77 — no objectively great idea, only ideas great for a channel at a stage) faces a much weaker version of it.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the video's promise a RECORD or a RECIPE — i.e. is the viewer's motive to witness an extreme (where the superlative IS the payload and must be literally true) or to solve a task they are currently mid-way through (where the number is proof of applicability, not scale)? And secondarily: is the channel large enough that a world-scope claim is credible from it at all? Creator Hooks (e41c5dcefb71) supplies the failure boundary — an implausible claim DEPRESSES clicks — which means the superlative rule is silently conditioned on the creator being able to actually deliver world scope.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: maker-builds rho=+0.149 (n=330, p=0.0062); roblox rho=+0.110 (n=378, p=0.033); motorcycle rho=+0.043 (n=406, p=0.39). Two of three niches positive and significant, the third neutral, none negative. The converse test agrees: titles whose subject is only a demonstrative or pronoun with no number show no lift anywhere (maker z=-0.84, moto z=-0.34, roblox z=+0.12).

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. The effect is small (rho ~0.11-0.15 explains ~1-2% of variance) and the proxy is imperfect: capitalised tokens also pick up brand names and game titles, so part of what I am measuring may be 'names a popular subject' rather than 'is specific'. Correlational only — a creator who writes specific titles may also make more specific videos. Notably the DIGIT form of specificity, which the claim names first, showed nothing (see 92005f0e083f).

Specific people, conditions, quantities, and results make an idea easier to understand and believe. Specificity often increases relevance even while narrowing the nominal audience.

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: roblox rho=-0.112 (n=378, p=0.028) — rarer vocabulary does associate with worse performance there. But motorcycle is -0.053 (p=0.29) and maker-builds is +0.035 (p=0.53). One niche out of three, at a p that would not survive correction for the number of features I tested.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Was the Eves case a face-vs-hands comparison at all, or a human-presence-vs-none comparison? Hands are human presence with a fusiform-adjacent salience of their own, so both observations are consistent with 'add a person to an object-only thumbnail' and inconsistent only about WHICH body part. The discriminating question is: does this channel's subscription proposition rest on the creator as a personality (face = recognition asset, and Trahan's consistent-expression theme in 98ed54ced350 compounds it) or on the object/outcome (hands keep the object at full size and put the viewer in first person)? Our corpus cannot settle it — the brief states we store thumbnail URLs but do not analyse pixels, and CTR is not exposed by the API at all.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Across 42 channels: 22 positive rho, 20 negative, median rho +0.005. Nine channels reach p<0.05 and they split both ways — Bikes and Beards +0.59, Aphmau Shuki +0.47, I did a thing +0.46, PrestonGamez +0.40, I Like To Make Stuff +0.42 against KreekCraft -0.75, RevZilla -0.61, CashBlox -0.42. Repeating your own title shape is neither reliably rewarded nor reliably punished in views.

Caveat: The claim's actual outcome variable is RETURNING VIEWERS, which we do not hold — YouTube's returning/new split is not in our data for any channel. A bucket strategy could genuinely build a returning audience while leaving total views flat (returning viewers substituting for browse reach), which is exactly what a null on views looks like. So this is a null on the wrong metric, and should be read as untested rather than refuted.

$1 Frappuccino versus Starbucks, $1 chicken sandwich versus Chick-fil-A, $1 pizza, $1 burrito. They're all the same thing. ... So by creating similar content, and I like to title them very similarly to just help and have similar metadata. So when YouTube sees that, they're going to know which videos to send back out. And that's how you create returning viewers.

Source: Yes Theory
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is length a CAUSE or a PROXY? Our own corpus says it is a proxy whose sign flips by niche — 'title over 60 chars' scores 0.90x vs 1.00x in maker-builds and 0.72x vs 1.00x in roblox, but 1.04x vs 0.97x in motorcycle (n=127, the largest cell in the table). The discriminating question is therefore: does this niche's demand arrive by BROWSE or by SEARCH? In browse-driven niches the long title is a symptom of two crammed concepts (Brag's actual mechanism) and reads as noise at feed size; in spec-driven search niches the extra characters are the brand/model/year the viewer typed, so length correlates with matching rather than with confusion. Reframe both claims as 'one concept per title' (causal) and drop the character count entirely (non-causal).

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Under-50-char titles do WORSE than longer ones in motorcycle: median 0.97x vs 1.03x, z=-2.08, p=0.038 (n=193 vs 213, 20 channels). Under-64 is the same story in motorcycle (0.97x vs 1.08x, z=-2.50, p=0.013). In roblox the rule points the other way — the 8 titles over 64 chars sit at 0.48x vs 1.00x (z=3.26, p=0.001). maker-builds is flat both ways (p=0.71, p=0.90). So the threshold helps in one niche, hurts in another, and does nothing in the third.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. n=8 for roblox's over-64 group is far too thin to carry weight on its own; the contradiction rests mainly on motorcycle running the wrong way with a decent sample. The 'ONE concept' half of the claim is not tested at all — I only measured character count. As with all these, CTR is unmeasured, so a title could win clicks and lose views.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Mean syllables per word vs outlier: maker-builds rho=+0.006 (p=0.91), motorcycle +0.125 (p=0.012), roblox +0.056 (p=0.28). Per-channel (42 channels, >=12 videos each): 25 positive, 17 negative, and the only 2 channels reaching p<0.05 are BOTH positive. Pooled buckets: simple titles (<1.35 syl/word) 0.995x, mid 0.970x, complex (>1.6) 1.060x. The one supportive signal is rare-word share in roblox (rho=-0.112, p=0.028) and it does not replicate in the other two niches.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. This is the sharpest CTR-vs-views gap in the whole set: the claim is explicitly about click-through rate, which we do not hold. Simpler titles could genuinely win more clicks while YouTube compensates with impressions, leaving views flat — our measure cannot separate those. What the data DOES rule out is the downstream inference that simplifying wording reliably produces more views. Syllable counting is also a crude complexity proxy and does not capture jargon-versus-plain-English substitution, which is the claim's actual mechanism.

Checked: Duration vs outlierScore: maker-builds rho=+0.103 (n=330, p=0.062), motorcycle +0.039 (p=0.43), roblox -0.076 (p=0.14). Per channel: 23 of 42 positive, 19 negative, 11 significant but split. Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The distribution IS heavy-tailed but not as extreme as the claim implies. Across 38 channels the median top-outlier is 3.85x the channel median; only 4 of 38 channels have any video at >=10x and exactly 1 (RevZilla, 104.5x) reaches >=100x. Max-over-p10 spread runs 6x to 387x. Inside the analysed cohorts max/median is 2.0x-10.5x and median/p10 only 1.2x-2.1x.

Caveat: The claim is a causal counterfactual — what the SAME video would have done with a better title — and nothing in observational view data can test it. What I can say is that the outcome distribution has enough tail to make 10x possible on roughly 1 channel in 10 and 100x on roughly 1 in 38, so the claim's headline numbers describe rare events, not the typical upside. Corpus channels are sampled at 15-40 videos each, which truncates the true tail and understates the maximum.

Checked: motorcycle: n=106 across 15 channels, median 1.01x vs 1.00x, z=0.68, p=0.50. roblox: n=11, p=0.79. maker-builds: n=5, too few. A separate brand+model pattern in motorcycle (n=113, 13 channels) gave 1.00x vs 1.00x, p=0.47. So there is no VIEWS lift — but the claim is specifically that CTR spikes while the impression pool stays small, which would produce exactly this flat views result.

Caveat: This is the clearest case where substituting outlier score for CTR would be dishonest: the claim predicts high CTR AND low impressions, whose product is ordinary views. Our flat result is consistent with the claim being true and with it being false. Only impressions-and-CTR data can settle it.

Checked: CTR is unavailable. The analogous retention pattern is strongly present: in 5 of 6 analysed channels the top-viewed video sits at or near the bottom of the retention ranking (10/10, 29/30, 9/9, 30/30, 26/30), and retention-vs-views rank correlations are negative and robust to duration control (-0.89 to -0.42). Caveat: I am deliberately not calling this supported. Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Pooled 17 of 39 top-retention videos sit in the bottom view tertile = 43.6%, against 33% by chance. Per channel: Channel F 2/3 (67%), Channel E 2/3 (67%), Channel C 4/10 (40%), Channel A 4/10 (40%), Channel D 4/10 (40%), Channel G 1/3 (33%). So the pattern is real and modestly over-represented — the videos the claim describes definitely exist in every channel we hold.

Caveat: Existence of the pattern is not the claim. The claim asserts a CAUSE (packaging, not content) and a REMEDY (repackage and relaunch), and we hold neither the CTR that would evidence the cause nor any before/after repackaging outcome that would evidence the remedy. An equally consistent explanation is that these are narrow-appeal videos that satisfied a small qualified audience — which is a content-scope decision, not a packaging fault. Small n per channel (3 videos in each tertile for the 9-10 video cohorts).

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What is the test FOR — ATTRIBUTION or CHOICE? A single-variable test answers 'what caused the lift' and needs everything else held constant; a shelf test answers 'which promise does a qualified viewer prefer against real competitors' and is worthless unless the options are genuinely distinct. They are also different instruments on different subjects: the shelf test is a preference test run on humans before filming, the A/B is an inference test run on the platform after publishing, and the dossier's warning about sequential testing (confounding audience, time, competition, seasonality, momentum) applies only to the second. Note that most of the store's repackaging advice — post-launch thumbnail swaps at 3a914075eefa, d56353b68dce, 49aa550ff948 — is sequential by construction and therefore sits inside the invalidity the dossier names, which nothing in the store currently acknowledges.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Was the Eves case a face-vs-hands comparison at all, or a human-presence-vs-none comparison? Hands are human presence with a fusiform-adjacent salience of their own, so both observations are consistent with 'add a person to an object-only thumbnail' and inconsistent only about WHICH body part. The discriminating question is: does this channel's subscription proposition rest on the creator as a personality (face = recognition asset, and Trahan's consistent-expression theme in 98ed54ced350 compounds it) or on the object/outcome (hands keep the object at full size and put the viewer in first person)? Our corpus cannot settle it — the brief states we store thumbnail URLs but do not analyse pixels, and CTR is not exposed by the API at all.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What does this audience believe it is buying — a spectacle, or a witness? Exaggeration is free where the genre contract is entertainment and the viewer expects heightening; it is a trust tax where the genre contract is 'this actually happened to a real person doing real work'. The operational form of the question: would a viewer who watched the video feel the thumbnail was a fair heightening of a moment that occurred (Galloway's own constraint in 7f11c9f5fbaa — it must look like a real screenshot from the video), or would they feel they were shown a thing that does not exist? The second discriminator is audience age, which c2c6c81bcc06 makes explicit and which nothing in the exaggeration camp controls for.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Sameness relative to WHAT — your own catalogue, or the feed you appear in? They are separate axes that the word 'consistency' collapses. Sameness with your own back catalogue is a recognition asset for a viewer who already liked one of them; sameness with the competitor beside you in the feed is indistinguishability. Gannett is reconcilable on the same split — familiarity removing avoidance IS Trahan's recognition effect, and the novel element is the video-specific variable inside the consistent shell. Our corpus supplies a live test of the second axis: in roblox, 322 of 378 videos carry an ALL-CAPS word and score 1.00x, while the 56 that do not score 1.07x. Where a convention is saturated, conformity is table stakes and the deviation carries the lift — meaning the value of any packaging feature depends on its BASE RATE in that niche's feed, not on an intrinsic effect. Reframe every packaging rule in the store as conditional on its local base rate.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: No packaging-change events are recorded in any store. The knowledge base holds one title and one thumbnail URL per video with no revision history, and the niche crawler upserts refresh view counts without versioning metadata. There is no hour-level view trajectory anywhere either — first-28d views is the finest window we hold.

Caveat: Even with a repackaging log, a single cited case would remain an anecdote with an unobservable counterfactual — the same video might have taken off anyway. The generalisable version of this claim (thumbnail swaps move views) is worth instrumenting; the specific 60k-to-3.9M figure is not verifiable by anyone but the original creator.

Theory packaging
When a repackage produces no movement, there are exactly two causes: the change was not different enough, or YouTube is withholding impressions because the video's watch-time-per-impression is below its bar — so a repackage cannot rescue a video that does not hold viewers.
Source: internal strategy session
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is retention being treated as a CAUSE of reach or as a SYMPTOM of audience narrowness? Our own data forces this question: retention-at-50% is NEGATIVELY rank-correlated with first-28d views on five of six channels we hold curves for (Channel C -0.45, Channel D -0.51, Channel E -0.85, Channel A -0.47, Channel F -0.89; Channel G +0.07). The videos that hold best are systematically the ones that reached fewest people. That is exactly what the the team audits describe from the other side (a85bd294e8c3, cc661b69dba9): reach expands the impression pool faster than click rate or hold rate can survive it, so a top video's low CTR and low retention are marks of broad distribution, not of weak packaging. The correct scoping is therefore: retention is a FLOOR (below the platform's bar, no packaging fixes anything — B is right), not a LEVER (above that floor, more retention buys no additional reach and packaging carries the outcome — A is right). Note our data cannot test the CTR half of either claim; the brief states CTR is not exposed by the API we use.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: No penalty is visible for a late top moment. Videos with the top peak after 60% (n=28): median APV 38.4%, median first-28d views 249,969. Videos with the top peak at or before 60% (n=61): median APV 38.7%, median first-28d views 221,408. Flagged peak positions overall are spread evenly across the runtime (p25 = 44%, median = 60%, p75 = 83%).

Caveat: This is the wrong shape of test for a claim about an intervention — comparing videos that HAPPEN to have a late peak against videos that happen to have an early one says nothing about what would happen if you moved content. Only an edit experiment can settle it. What the comparison does show is that a late top moment is not, by itself, a marker of a weaker video, which removes the diagnostic urgency the claim implies.

Where the claim came from
Its guidance suggests moving compelling content earlier when top moments occur late and creating new content by expanding top moments.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The data points the other way: rho(first-15s loss, first-28d views) is negative in 6/6 channels — Channel C -0.54, Channel D -0.45, Channel F -0.45, Channel E -0.37, Channel A -0.03, Channel G -0.04; pooled -0.32. Videos that got more views lost FEWER viewers in the opening. Median first-15s loss is also tightly clustered (6.5-9.4% across channels, worst single video 16.2%), so 'hockey stick' cliffs are rare in this set.

Caveat: Properly testing this needs CTR and impressions, which we do not hold — views conflate demand, delivery and click-rate, so a negative cliff-views correlation is not the same as a negative cliff-CTR correlation. The counter-signal is suggestive, not decisive. Note also that our channels simply may not produce the hockey-stick pathology: with a worst-case 16% first-15s loss, there may be no genuine instances of the phenomenon in the sample to diagnose.

Theory retention · earlier check spanned 6 channels Contested
Announcing the end of a video is what causes the terminal retention cliff - viewers leave the moment they perceive the core content is finished, so the transition to the next video must happen before any wrap-up signal.
Source: Sean Cannell
Contested — what would settle it

Which objective is being optimised — SESSION continuation (next-video click-through and watch time in this sitting) or REPEAT viewership (whether this viewer opens the channel's next upload)? These pull opposite ways at the outro, and each source is silently optimising a different one. The store's own 4214845e0b40 (Joos: under-delivering on a teased reward drives dopamine below baseline and suppresses willingness to wait in FUTURE videos) says the cost of the hand-off lands on later uploads, which is exactly the metric the retention curve cannot see. Restated: (a) optimising session watch time → hand off before the wrap-up signal; (b) optimising return rate on future uploads → resolve cleanly, and only then offer the next video. UNTESTABLE IN OUR DATA — we hold no next-video click-through or per-viewer return data.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: A terminal cliff is real and large in 6/6 channels. Final-10% loss (median): Channel G 35.3%, Channel C 28.1%, Channel D 23.0%, Channel F 22.4%, Channel E 14.1%, Channel A 9.4%. The matched mid-video 10% band loses far less: Channel C 1.1%, Channel F 3.0%, Channel G 2.2%, Channel E 2.0%, Channel D 10.6%, Channel A 9.2%. Per video, final-10% loss exceeds mid-10% loss in 97 of 119 cases. Median hazard by band is U-shaped: highest at 1-5%, ~0 through 46-90%, then rising again at 91-100%.

Caveat: The cliff exists; the stated CAUSE does not follow from it. We have no labelling of where a wrap-up signal occurs, so we cannot separate 'the creator announced the end' from the trivially expected fact that people stop watching when a video is over, from end-cards, from outros, or from the curve's own end artefact. The 3.7x spread between Channel A (9.4%) and Channel G (35.3%) shows the cliff size is not fixed, which is at least consistent with an editorial cause — but that is a hint, not a test.

Disputed

Opposite instructions for the same closing 20 seconds: suppress resolution and hand off to the next video, versus resolve cleanly and do not tease forward. Both are act-on-able and mutually exclusive.

Settle it by answering: Which objective is being optimised — SESSION continuation (next-video click-through and watch time in this sitting) or REPEAT viewership (whether this viewer opens the channel's next upload)? These pull opposite ways at the outro, and each source is silently optimising a different one. The store's own 4214845e0b40 (Joos: under-delivering on a teased reward drives dopamine below baseline and suppresses willingness to wait in FUTURE videos) says the cost of the hand-off lands on later uploads, which is exactly the metric the retention curve cannot see. Restated: (a) optimising session watch time → hand off before the wrap-up signal; (b) optimising return rate on future uploads → resolve cleanly, and only then offer the next video. UNTESTABLE IN OUR DATA — we hold no next-video click-through or per-viewer return data.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Naively the claim looks overwhelming: the first flagged drop is the largest in 99/99 videos, median hazard by order 15.3% -> -0.5% -> -1.0% -> -1.4%. But this is an artefact — the p25 of flagged drop positions is 1.0% of runtime, so 'first drop' is overwhelmingly 'the intro drop', which we already know is the biggest drop in 97% of videos. Excluding the first 10% of runtime leaves only 12 qualifying videos, and there the first post-intro drop is the largest in 6 of 12 — barely above chance, with median hazard by order 1.1% -> 0.0% -> -0.9%.

Caveat: Two blocking problems. (1) We have no ground-truth segment boundaries; flagged drops are our own model's output and are selected for being drops, which biases every comparison. (2) Once the intro is removed the usable sample collapses to 12 videos. This needs segment labelling before it can be judged.

Evidence and caveats →
Bound to a test, awaiting data

This claim IS measurable and has been written as a lever: opening the sponsor read by naming the sponsor → audience lost across the sponsor segment, expected to go up. It is tested by asking: Do sponsor reads that open by naming the sponsor bleed more of the audience than reads that open some other way? No analysed channel has yet had enough data for that test to return a number — every probe stays silent below its minimum sample rather than reporting a figure that would look like evidence. It will be measured automatically on the next run that qualifies.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: 42 flagged moments mention a sponsor; 32 of them (76%) are drops and 10 are peaks. So sponsor segments do disproportionately coincide with flagged losses in our cohort, and are not universally negative.

Caveat: This cannot test the claim's actual mechanism, which is about WHERE inside the read the brand name lands. We do not have per-read transcripts aligned to disclosure position, and 42 moments is thin. Worse, the sample is selection-biased in both directions: moments are surfaced only when the curve does something notable, so a sponsor read that held perfectly is invisible here, while a read placed near an unrelated drop gets credited with it. The 10 sponsor-adjacent PEAKS are worth noting against the assumption that ad reads always cost retention, but they are equally subject to that bias.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the phrase carry INFORMATION about what is withheld, or is it a bare instruction? The store supplies its own resolving mechanism in aad4e27d043c (Joos): curiosity peaks at PARTIAL information — enough to guess, not enough to be certain — which is exactly why a contentless 'watch till the end' fails while a named, specific withheld item ('the bonus tip', 'the price') creates a live question. Restated: (a) name the withheld thing specifically enough to be guessable → works; (b) issue a bare instruction to stay → does nothing.

Restated: (a) thumbnail shows the finished object → first frame must partially deliver it; (b) thumbnail poses a feasibility question → withhold the object, show the plan.

Restated: (a) new flat + total rising → benign, do not chase TAM; (b) new flat + total flat → reach ceiling, escalate topic TAM and packaging.

Bound to a test, awaiting data

This claim IS measurable and has been written as a lever: opening a sponsor read by naming the sponsor → audience lost across the sponsor read, expected to go up. It is tested by asking: Do sponsor reads that open by naming the sponsor bleed more of the audience than reads that open some other way? No analysed channel has yet had enough data for that test to return a number — every probe stays silent below its minimum sample rather than reporting a figure that would look like evidence. It will be measured automatically on the next run that qualifies.

Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — which is exactly why it sits at Theory rather than higher — the rung means the cause and effect behind it has not been quantified. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Checked: We hold none of the three. Our knowledge base stores curves, flagged moments and transcripts-as-quotes, but no labelled sponsor spans and no structural classification of how a read was edited. Only 42 flagged moments across the whole 119-video cohort mention a sponsor at all, none of them labelled by read structure.

Caveat: This is testable in principle with our pipeline — the segment census in src/lib/analysis/segments.ts already clusters sponsor reads from transcript cues and measures bleed depth — but it would need a read-structure label added and enough labelled instances to compare. Nothing in the current store supports the 10-20% vs 2% contrast, in either direction.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the sponsor cue LABEL A SKIPPABLE BLOCK, and how long is that block? The cue is only costly when it tells the viewer how much runtime to jump. A 2-4 second standalone tag has no block behind it (and the 5-second skip granularity overshoots into content), while the same words opening a 60-90 second integration are a precise skip instruction. Restated: (a) a sub-5-second disclosure with no segment behind it is safe anywhere, including the top; (b) any disclosure that opens a segment longer than the skip granularity must be moved to the segment's end.

Source: Mario Joos (retention courses)
Contested — what would settle it

Which objective is being optimised — SESSION continuation (next-video click-through and watch time in this sitting) or REPEAT viewership (whether this viewer opens the channel's next upload)? These pull opposite ways at the outro, and each source is silently optimising a different one. The store's own 4214845e0b40 (Joos: under-delivering on a teased reward drives dopamine below baseline and suppresses willingness to wait in FUTURE videos) says the cost of the hand-off lands on later uploads, which is exactly the metric the retention curve cannot see. Restated: (a) optimising session watch time → hand off before the wrap-up signal; (b) optimising return rate on future uploads → resolve cleanly, and only then offer the next video. UNTESTABLE IN OUR DATA — we hold no next-video click-through or per-viewer return data.

Disputed

Opposite instructions for the same closing 20 seconds: suppress resolution and hand off to the next video, versus resolve cleanly and do not tease forward. Both are act-on-able and mutually exclusive.

Settle it by answering: Which objective is being optimised — SESSION continuation (next-video click-through and watch time in this sitting) or REPEAT viewership (whether this viewer opens the channel's next upload)? These pull opposite ways at the outro, and each source is silently optimising a different one. The store's own 4214845e0b40 (Joos: under-delivering on a teased reward drives dopamine below baseline and suppresses willingness to wait in FUTURE videos) says the cost of the hand-off lands on later uploads, which is exactly the metric the retention curve cannot see. Restated: (a) optimising session watch time → hand off before the wrap-up signal; (b) optimising return rate on future uploads → resolve cleanly, and only then offer the next video. UNTESTABLE IN OUR DATA — we hold no next-video click-through or per-viewer return data.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The knowledge base stores a single current subscriberCount per channel and no historical series. Analysed cohorts span only 4-22 months of uploads per channel, over which no channel in the set crossed a scale boundary we could detect. There is no before/after pairing available.

Caveat: This claim, if true, would materially limit the shelf life of every finding in this exercise — including the negative retention-views correlation, which was measured on channels at 54k-988k median views and might not hold at 10M. It deserves flagging as an unresolved threat to all of the above rather than being quietly filed as untestable.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the video's promise turn on WHETHER IT WORKS (feasibility — withholding preserves the question) or on WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE (spectacle — proof of delivery is the click-confirmation), and does the thumbnail already show the finished object? If the thumbnail shows it, withholding is impossible and reads as a bait-and-switch; if the thumbnail poses a question, showing the object closes it. Restated: (a) thumbnail shows the finished object → first frame must partially deliver it; (b) thumbnail poses a feasibility question → withhold the object, show the plan.

A real test needs an independent judgement of segment strength, which we do not have.

Checked: The associative half reproduces in 6/6 channels: rho(introLoss, end retention) = -0.79 Channel C, -0.24 Channel D, -0.63 Channel E, -0.52 Channel A, -0.27 Morley, -0.55 Zac. Videos that hold the opening hold the ending. But genuine peaks essentially never occur in the first decile (0% of 96 Channel C peaks, 0% of 85 Channel D, 0% of 33 Channel E, 3% of 36 Channel A); peak medians sit at 54%, 59%, 90% and 62% of duration. So on six healthy channels the strongest rewind-worthy moment is systematically NOT first.

Caveat: The correlation is almost certainly confounded by audience composition: a video pushed to a colder browse audience loses more early AND holds less throughout, which produces this pattern with no primacy effect at all. And the peak evidence cannot falsify the prescription — an opening that simply holds well produces no rewind spike, so absence of early peaks is not evidence of a weak opening. Causal claim, correlational data only.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which outcome is this video being built for — SESSION CONTINUATION or PROPAGATION? Joos's peak-end argument optimises the memory trace and the state the viewer is in when the next thumbnail appears: leave them elevated and they click. Eves and Gordon are optimising for what leaves the platform — the beat a viewer can retell, and the reflective residue that produces a comment. These are different currencies and a channel usually needs one more than the other. The second variable is whether the extra beat is a DECOMPRESSION (arousal decays — Joos is right) or a NEW small payoff (arousal is re-spiked before the cut — Eves's 'gush' is not an ease-out at all, which may dissolve half this conflict). We can measure the shape of the last 5% of the curve; we hold no shares or comment data, so the propagation half is untestable here.

Checked: Outros are expensive everywhere: median 95-100% hazard per 1% of video is 4.63% (Channel C), 3.49% (Channel D), 3.47% (Channel E), 3.89% (Morley), 5.47% (Zac), against 0.03-0.75% in the 60-90% band — the terminal band is the steepest post-intro band in 77-100% of videos on 5 of 6 channels. But the downstream half returns nothing: rho(end-hold_i, early-hold of next upload) = -0.21, -0.00, -0.02, -0.09, -0.35, -0.55 across 113 pairs, i.e. no benefit in the predicted direction.

Caveat: We cannot measure outro LENGTH, which is the actual variable — an abrupt cut and an extended wind-down both show up only as a terminal hazard number, and end cards inflate that number for every video regardless. The downstream null is the same test that refuted be6d7777d2f3 and shares its weakness: first-28d views and early retention on the next upload are dominated by packaging and distribution.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the front-loaded item NAVIGATION or PAYLOAD? A roadmap ('there are three attempts, the last one is the hard one') costs the viewer nothing to hold — it is a promise about order and it reduces the uncertainty that causes drift. A rule, a spec, a name, a constraint is payload: the viewer must retain it to understand a later beat, and they will not. So the repaired pair of rules is: front-load the SHAPE, never the CONTENT; anything the viewer must remember gets revealed at the moment it becomes load-bearing, with a visual. This is the cleanest scope repair in the store and it is entirely inside one source.

Bound to a test, awaiting data

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Median first-peak position: Channel C 47%, Channel D 38%, Channel E 52%, Channel A 44% of duration. rho(first-peak position, retention at 75%) = +0.04 Channel C, +0.21 Channel D, -0.13 Channel E, -0.61 Channel A. Two channels lean the predicted way, two lean the opposite, and the largest coefficient runs AGAINST the claim. rho against views is likewise scattered (-0.12, -0.14, +0.05, +0.20).

Caveat: A rewind peak is not the same thing as the narrative payoff — our peak detector finds moments viewers scrubbed back to, which can be a mid-video reveal, a joke, or a technical detail. Without labelled climax timestamps this proxy is weak, and the 9-30 video within-channel samples cannot carry a modest effect anyway.

Theory storytelling · earlier check spanned 4 channels
Great videos place a bonus beat ('the gush') AFTER the climax and before the wrap-up, which is what viewers repeat to friends - so the video should not end at its payoff.
Source: Derrel Eves
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which outcome is this video being built for — SESSION CONTINUATION or PROPAGATION? Joos's peak-end argument optimises the memory trace and the state the viewer is in when the next thumbnail appears: leave them elevated and they click. Eves and Gordon are optimising for what leaves the platform — the beat a viewer can retell, and the reflective residue that produces a comment. These are different currencies and a channel usually needs one more than the other. The second variable is whether the extra beat is a DECOMPRESSION (arousal decays — Joos is right) or a NEW small payoff (arousal is re-spiked before the cut — Eves's 'gush' is not an ease-out at all, which may dissolve half this conflict). We can measure the shape of the last 5% of the curve; we hold no shares or comment data, so the propagation half is untestable here.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the payoff exist independently of the shoot, and can this production afford coverage? Khare's format is a designed challenge with an engineered payoff — the outcome is the plan, so shooting without a thesis means missing the shots the payoff needs. Yes Theory's subject is a PERSON or a PLACE whose behaviour is the content, and no thesis can predict it. The economics discriminate too: Brag's 3f346d2d855c says Yes Theory shoots 30-40 mini-scenes and keeps ~18 — a coverage ratio that makes discovery affordable. A single-run challenge with one take cannot buy that option. And Brag himself supplies the guard rail (c07117b89994): the Iceman documentary had to be fully recut because an editing team forced real events into a planned arc — so the failure both sources agree on is a plan that survives contact with contradicting footage.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Weak and inconsistent: maker-builds 1.15x with (n=12) vs 1.00x without (n=318), delta +0.15; roblox 1.07x (n=10) vs 1.00x (n=368), +0.07; motorcycle 1.01x (n=28) vs 1.00x (n=378), +0.01. The direction is positive in all three niches but the two larger samples show essentially nothing, and the largest delta rests on 12 videos.

Caveat: The TAM half of the claim is flatly untestable here — it turns on impressions, which the API path we use does not expose, so we cannot distinguish 'more people watched' from 'more people were SHOWN it'. Emotional-stakes keywords in a title are also a thin proxy for an emotional beat inside the video, and outlier score is a within-channel views ratio that cannot separate reach from resonance.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the front-loaded item NAVIGATION or PAYLOAD? A roadmap ('there are three attempts, the last one is the hard one') costs the viewer nothing to hold — it is a promise about order and it reduces the uncertainty that causes drift. A rule, a spec, a name, a constraint is payload: the viewer must retain it to understand a later beat, and they will not. So the repaired pair of rules is: front-load the SHAPE, never the CONTENT; anything the viewer must remember gets revealed at the moment it becomes load-bearing, with a visual. This is the cleanest scope repair in the store and it is entirely inside one source.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: It requires two independent human or model scores per video — narrative structure and edit polish — regressed against AVD. We store neither score, and generating them from our own pipeline would be circular: the moment findings were written by a model already primed with the audit's storytelling priors, so its structural judgements cannot serve as an independent regressor against its own retention explanations.

Caveat: None — data gap. Worth noting the circularity risk applies to any claim we might be tempted to test using the WHAT/WHY/HOW text as a label rather than as an observation.

Source: Jonathan Hurwitz (10 years at Disney/Pixar)
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Has the audience already COMMITTED to finishing? Joos names the discriminator himself in 4ad699f1dd60: the YouTube intro's job is context and the rules of the world, not character exposition, 'because viewers arrive without any commitment to finish, unlike film audiences.' A cinema audience has paid and cannot leave, so early backstory is an investment; a YouTube viewer is auditing and early backstory is an unpaid bill. The second variable is what the backstory is FOR — Pixar needed the viewer to LIKE a character they would spend 100 minutes with; a YouTube creator's 'why I'm doing this' is usually a justification the viewer has not yet asked for. Our own data locates the exact edge: median retention at 15s is 91.9-94.2% across all six analysed channels but falls to 72-79% by 30s (Channel E excepted at 93.5%). The first 15 seconds are nearly free; the bill lands between 15s and 60s. That is direct support for our strategist's 353818aee0a4 placement of the emotional WHY at 15-20s — after the free window, before the cliff.

Ceiling estimation must separate reachable demand from total popularity by counting recent qualified videos, their NORMALIZED performance, and how many materially similar versions already exist — raw topic popularity overstates the opportunity.
Source: idea-engine research dossier
Evidence and caveats →
Not measurable by anything we currently compute

No test in our battery measures this claim's variables, so it has never been quantified — which is exactly why it sits at Theory rather than higher — the rung means the cause and effect behind it has not been quantified. Our probes run over retention curves, runtime, publish dates, view counts, titles and detected intro / sponsor / payoff / outro segments. Claims about click-through rate, impressions, thumbnails, subscriber behaviour, revenue or a viewer's internal motive are outside that reach.

Binding it to a loosely-related test would be worse than leaving it unmeasured: it would attach a real number to the wrong question, and that number would move this claim's standing.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: No relationship: rho(cluster supply, cluster median outlier) = -0.02 across 53 clusters. If anything supply runs the other way — high-supply clusters (15+ videos, n=6) have a median outlier of 1.17x against 1.02x for low-supply clusters (5-7 videos, n=35). The largest cluster, 'animal hospital' (49 videos), medians 1.28x; 'meccha chameleon' (22 videos) medians 1.21x. Only 'motorcycle camping' (24 videos, 0.89x) fits the claim.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. The proxy is crude and this verdict should not be over-read. Bigram clusters are not 'materially similar versions', and I could not impose the claim's 90-day recency restriction — the corpus spans years of publish dates. Crowded subjects here are crowded because they WORK (a popular Roblox game attracts both supply and demand), so supply and demand are entangled in a way this test cannot separate. Read this as: our data gives no support for a supply penalty, not as proof that saturation never hurts.

Where the claim came from
Separate reachable demand from total popularity. Count recent qualified videos, their normalized performance, and how many materially similar versions already exist.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Absolute views and outlier score are only weakly related (rho +0.28), and channel size is orthogonal to outlier magnitude (rho(channel median views, outlier score) = -0.03) — so a big channel does not manufacture big outlier scores. Of the top decile by ABSOLUTE views (n=112, all above 2.31M views), 64% score below 1.5x on their own channel. Conversely, of the 62 videos at 3x+ their own baseline, 39% have below-corpus-median absolute views.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. This establishes that the two rankings are largely independent — it does NOT establish that the normalised one is better DEMAND evidence, which is the claim's actual assertion. Testing that would require following a topic from a small-channel breakout to a later large-channel attempt, which we have no data for. The corpus is peer/trending/search collected, so channels are not a random sample and outlier scores rest on however many videos we happened to collect per channel (median well under 30).

Where the claim came from
A 100,000-view upload on a channel normally earning 10,000 may be more informative than a 1,000,000-view upload on a channel normally earning 900,000.

Checked: Mean exceeds median in 6/6 channels, by 1.12x to 2.46x. Channel E is the clear case: median 691,316 vs mean 1,699,820 (2.46x), because one 10.5x breakout drags the mean; a mean-normalised score would call only 2 of 9 videos above baseline where the median calls 4 of 9. Channel C: mean/median 1.36x, 7 vs 15 videos above baseline. Across the 1,114-video niche corpus, channel median views is essentially uncorrelated with outlier score (rho -0.03), confirming the normaliser is doing channel-size removal correctly.

Caveat: [superseded] computed on the age-confounded outlier score; 6 of 15 title-feature effects flip sign under age control, so this result cannot be distinguished from accumulation bias. Re-test now that scoring is age-normalised. This verifies median-over-mean and confirms the normaliser removes channel size. It does NOT verify the specific prescriptions of 10-20 videos or 'at the same age window' — we did not vary N, and our own scores already use a first-28d window, so the age-window rule is assumed rather than tested. The subscriber-count half is untestable: we hold subscriber counts for only 3 of 7 channels.

Where the claim came from
Use the median views of roughly 10-20 recent comparable uploads at the same age window. Record subscribers only as context; channel baseline is the more useful normalizer.

Checked: Neither CTR nor impressions is held. The only structurally analogous quantity we can measure is APV against views, which does decline as views rise (pooled rho -0.54, 6/6 channels) — consistent with the dilution mechanism the claim describes, but on a different metric.

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: (a) Premise holds: Channel D' 30 videos span 671 days at 23 d/video; Channel E's 9 span 616 days at 77 d/video. (b) The 'stale data' consequence does not show up. Dropping videos older than 12 months moves the channel's median 28d views by only +4% (Channel D), -2% (Channel F), -11% (Channel E), -13% (Channel G). Median APV barely moves for Channel D (31.4% recent vs 30.9% older). Three channels have no video older than 12 months, so no split is possible.

Caveat: The test is weak where it matters: only Channel D has a sizeable older group (13 videos), and Channel E/Channel F/Channel G have 4, 1 and 2 respectively — far too few to compare distributions. Recency also correlates with views inconsistently across channels (rho -0.44 to +0.16), so there is no single ageing effect to detect. A channel with a genuine three-year window and a real audience shift could still be badly served by a fixed N; we simply do not hold one.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The premise holds firmly: 30-second retention does not determine views. rho(30s retention, 28d views) is -0.50, -0.33, -0.29, -0.19, +0.26, +0.37 across the six channels — no consistent sign. Among matched pairs the surviving view gap is large: Channel C 69 pairs, median 1.26x and up to 2.0x; Channel D 34 pairs, median 1.54x, up to 4.7x; Channel G 9 pairs, median 1.67x; Channel E 6 pairs, median 3.58x, up to 17.6x.

Caveat: Everything except the causal attribution checks out. We can show that equal 30-second holding leaves views nearly unexplained; we CANNOT show the residual is packaging. We hold no CTR, no impressions, and no traffic-source split, so topic demand, seasonality, algorithmic timing and subject breadth are all folded into that residual alongside packaging. Treat the pattern as 'watchability did not cause the gap' — not as 'packaging did'.

Theory analytics · earlier check spanned 6 channels Contested
A video with high retention but low views has a PACKAGING problem, not a content problem — the retention proves the video can hold a wider audience than the packaging reached, so it is the prime repackaging candidate.
Source: internal strategy session
Contested — what would settle it

Is the video's retention high in ABSOLUTE terms, or high as a RESIDUAL — above what the channel's own retention-versus-views relationship predicts at that view count? Only the residual carries information; the absolute number is confounded by exactly the mechanism claim B names. OUR DATA SETTLES THIS: rank correlation between retention-at-50% and first-28d views is -0.45 (Channel C), -0.51 (Channel D), -0.85 (Channel E), -0.47 (Channel A), -0.89 (Channel F), +0.07 (Channel G) — negative on 5 of 6 channels, strongly so on the two small-n maker channels. The repackaging rule must therefore be re-specified as 'retention above the channel's fitted expectation at that view count', and the existing verdict table in our own pipeline should be checked against this.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: The quadrant is the DEFAULT, not a diagnosis: among below-median-view videos, the share that also sit above median APV is Channel C 60%, Channel D 60%, Channel A 73%, Channel F 80%, Channel G 80%, Channel E 100%. This is forced by the underlying negative views/retention correlation (pooled -0.54) — low-view videos are ALSO the high-retention ones almost by construction, so the rule flags 60-100% of every channel's underperformers and discriminates almost nothing.

Caveat: Two separate problems. First, no repackage outcomes exist in our data, so the causal claim ('retention proves it can hold a wider audience') is untestable — retention was measured on the narrow audience it actually reached, and there is no evidence it would survive a wider one; the negative views/retention correlation is direct evidence against exactly that extrapolation. Second, even as a screening heuristic the rule barely narrows the field. The team's existing 'repackage or double down' verdict table, which ranks retention-at-50% AGAINST first-28d views rather than thresholding both, is the sounder version of this idea.

Disputed

Same speaker. If retention falls mechanically as views rise, then 'high retention + low views' is largely the ARITHMETIC CONSEQUENCE of low views, not independent evidence of watchability — so the repackaging filter is selecting on the artefact the second claim describes. As written the filter would nominate nearly every low-view video on the channel.

Settle it by answering: Is the video's retention high in ABSOLUTE terms, or high as a RESIDUAL — above what the channel's own retention-versus-views relationship predicts at that view count? Only the residual carries information; the absolute number is confounded by exactly the mechanism claim B names. OUR DATA SETTLES THIS: rank correlation between retention-at-50% and first-28d views is -0.45 (Channel C), -0.51 (Channel D), -0.85 (Channel E), -0.47 (Channel A), -0.89 (Channel F), +0.07 (Channel G) — negative on 5 of 6 channels, strongly so on the two small-n maker channels. The repackaging rule must therefore be re-specified as 'retention above the channel's fitted expectation at that view count', and the existing verdict table in our own pipeline should be checked against this.

Theory analytics
New-viewer counts are structurally suppressed by successful conversion: each new viewer who becomes a returning viewer vacates a slot that must be refilled, so flat new-viewer numbers during strong returning growth do NOT mean acquisition has stopped.
Source: our own channel audits
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

What did TOTAL views and impressions do over the same window? Flat new-viewer count with RISING totals is the accounting artefact of conversion (the cohort is being reclassified, not lost); flat new-viewer count with FLAT OR FALLING totals is a genuine reach ceiling. Restated: (a) new flat + total rising → benign, do not chase TAM; (b) new flat + total flat → reach ceiling, escalate topic TAM and packaging.

Theory analytics Contested
Despite CTR decaying with reach, first-hour and first-24-hour CTR is strongly correlated with long-term video performance on established channels — so early CTR is the usable predictive signal even though lifetime CTR is not.
Source: Paddy Galloway
Contested — what would settle it

Is day-one CTR read as an ABSOLUTE number or as a residual against the SAME channel's own prior day-one CTRs, and is that channel's day-one audience compositionally stable? Paddy's claim is scoped to established channels, where day one is a near-constant subscriber-heavy panel — that stability is what makes the comparison legitimate. Joos's counterexample is impression-accumulation rate varying per video, which corrupts absolute readings. Note the store already carries a partial carve-out from Joos himself (4f18d60d2b00: on news and patch-update channels day-one behaviour genuinely does carry signal). UNTESTABLE IN OUR DATA — we hold no CTR or impressions at all.
