Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Across 46 channels and 1,290 videos: 76 within-channel format families reach 2+ uses, 15 reach 4+, only 3 reach 10+, and ZERO reach 20 (largest run = 14). In the mined format library the median matchCount is 3, the maximum is 27, and only 2 of 57 formats reach 20 matches — and those pool multiple channels.

Caveat: Our per-channel windows are ~25-40 recent uploads, so a format that ran 20 episodes over five years would be truncated — the count is a floor, not a ceiling. More importantly the claim is about a PLANNING exercise (can you imagine 20?), not a shipping target, so a low observed shipping count does not refute it; it only says that if 20 shipped episodes is the implied standard, essentially nothing in our corpus meets it.

Theory strategy · earlier check spanned 46 channels
Frequent format-switching starves the recommendation system of the patterns it needs to identify an audience, so the channel becomes unroutable rather than merely slow-growing.
Source: Derrel Eves
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the channel's growth currently coming from NEW algorithmic reach or from an existing audience returning — and what is the audience actually attached to? Eves's mechanism is a classifier problem (a machine needs a repeated pattern to find lookalike viewers) and only binds while the channel still needs to be discovered. Kandil's mechanism is a churn problem and only binds once an audience exists that can leave. The two truths are sequential, not opposed: hold the format while the algorithm is still learning who you are; build a stated value on top of it before the format ages. The test for which regime you are in is whether returning-viewer share is still climbing or has plateaued.

The 64M-view anecdote is a single video on a channel we do not hold; single-video before/after evidence cannot separate timing from the video itself.

Theory strategy · earlier check spanned 13 channels
A channel should retire its signature device BEFORE performance declines, because the decline is caused by accumulated exposure, not by the device becoming worse.
Source: Alan Garnett
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the device a RECOGNITION marker or a NOVELTY device — and is the repetition within one video or across many? Two separate scopes are collapsed here. (1) Within a video, repetition is dead time the viewer has already paid for; across videos, the same repetition is what makes the channel identifiable in a feed. Joos's own two claims resolve on exactly that axis. (2) A device whose effect is RECOGNITION (a font, a set, a returning theme) does not fatigue — Gannett's own 180d93548c26 exempts habit-forming products from the exposure curve. A device whose effect depends on SURPRISE (a running gag, an escalating stunt, a signature reveal) does fatigue, and Gannett's retire-early rule applies only to it. The operational test: if removing it would make a regular viewer fail to recognise the channel, it is recognition — hold it. If removing it would make them notice nothing, it was novelty and is already spent. Gannett's b9b71a3fb0a1 adds the timing guard: core-audience boredom arrives before mainstream discovery, so core complaints are not the retirement signal.

Checked: Median spearman(repetition index, age-adjusted performance) = -0.20, with 9 families negative and 5 positive. Early half of a run: median residual -0.007 (n=42); later half -0.074 (n=46); Mann-Whitney p=0.144. The unadjusted number is -0.34, but that is inflated by video age and should not be quoted.

Caveat: Directionally consistent with exposure fatigue but not significant, and badly underpowered — 15 families is not enough to separate fatigue from the ordinary decline of any channel's mid-list ideas. Title-signature families are a coarse stand-in for a 'signature device' (a recurring segment, catchphrase or editing motif is invisible in a title). The claim's actionable half — that retiring EARLY beats retiring on decline — needs cases of deliberate retirement, which we cannot identify at all.

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does this footage support SIX DISTINCT PROMISES, or one promise cut into six pieces? Khare is right about PARTS — a part-two inherits a weakened package and asks the viewer to have seen part one. The packet's six are not parts: 'packing' and 'campsite ranking' are separate questions with separate titles, separate thumbnails and partly separate audiences, and none of them requires the others. So the rule is not about count at all, it is about whether each upload has an independent, clickable promise that stands alone. The store also supplies the failure mode at the other extreme: Channel I's c112e6452da9 — 30 daily uploads bought a subscriber bump then flatlined by day 30 as reach fell back to the core (~125k average down to 30-40k), which is what happens when the pieces have no independent promise. our strategist's 5e3bd00115b5 (2-4 long-form from a month-long trip) sits between the two and is the operating compromise.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which surface is this channel's long-form distribution actually coming from, and what is the GAP between the two uploads? The cannibalisation mechanism is freshness ranking within a single channel's slot on the subscriber home feed — it binds hard on a channel whose long-form views are subscriber-fed and barely at all on one fed by suggested/search. The second missing variable is time: 'the day after' is not the same decision as 'four days later'. Reframe both as one conditional: if long-form is home-feed-fed, Shorts are cadence-fillers only in the trough between uploads, never inside the freshness window; if it is suggested-fed, the medium genuinely does not compete. We cannot test this — traffic-source splits are not exposed by the API we use.

Source: our own channel audits
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is this an EPISODE or a TENTPOLE? Hurwitz's 5cb5e965b040 already draws the line: regular uploads are episodes of an open-ended series, tentpoles are finite films, and the two require different structures. An episodic container has slack — the metric can legitimately set the dial because the format can absorb another segment. A tentpole's length is determined by its payoff, and cutting to hit a number breaks the thing people came for. Our own data supports the audits' direction within episodic catalogues: the longer half of the catalogue won on median first-28d views for six of seven channels (Channel C 321,662 vs 291,465; Channel D 65,205 vs 48,143; Channel A 251,961 vs 218,645; Channel F 1,012,676 vs 963,861; Channel B 287,063 vs 207,873; Channel G 485,039 vs 367,785). The single exception is Channel E — the channel with by far the longest median duration at 52 minutes — where longer LOST (691,316 vs 863,878). That is the shape of a permission-to-lengthen rule with a channel-specific ceiling, not a universal one, and it is why the rule must be re-read each quarter rather than applied once.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the device a RECOGNITION marker or a NOVELTY device — and is the repetition within one video or across many? Two separate scopes are collapsed here. (1) Within a video, repetition is dead time the viewer has already paid for; across videos, the same repetition is what makes the channel identifiable in a feed. Joos's own two claims resolve on exactly that axis. (2) A device whose effect is RECOGNITION (a font, a set, a returning theme) does not fatigue — Gannett's own 180d93548c26 exempts habit-forming products from the exposure curve. A device whose effect depends on SURPRISE (a running gag, an escalating stunt, a signature reveal) does fatigue, and Gannett's retire-early rule applies only to it. The operational test: if removing it would make a regular viewer fail to recognise the channel, it is recognition — hold it. If removing it would make them notice nothing, it was novelty and is already spent. Gannett's b9b71a3fb0a1 adds the timing guard: core-audience boredom arrives before mainstream discovery, so core complaints are not the retirement signal.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Which surface is this channel's long-form distribution actually coming from, and what is the GAP between the two uploads? The cannibalisation mechanism is freshness ranking within a single channel's slot on the subscriber home feed — it binds hard on a channel whose long-form views are subscriber-fed and barely at all on one fed by suggested/search. The second missing variable is time: 'the day after' is not the same decision as 'four days later'. Reframe both as one conditional: if long-form is home-feed-fed, Shorts are cadence-fillers only in the trough between uploads, never inside the freshness window; if it is suggested-fed, the medium genuinely does not compete. We cannot test this — traffic-source splits are not exposed by the API we use.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the 'experiment' vary an INPUT inside the preserved viewer contract, or vary the contract itself? The ideation packet already supplies the discipline (8ab1156f2655: the second episode of a candidate format preserves the structure and changes exactly one major input). Joos's experimental slot is coherent only if the promised transformation is held constant and the topic, cast, constraint or setting is what moves; Chaudry's punished video is one where the transformation itself changed. So the missing context is: what does this audience's return depend on — the WORLD (creator, cast, recurring frame, where a new topic is welcome) or the TRANSFORMATION (a specific outcome they came for, where a new topic reads as a bait-and-switch)? Ask which of the two the channel's top comments are about.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Subscriber counts exist only for the 7 knowledge-base channels, not for the 46 corpus channels, and no channel in the store has a growth time series — the corpus is a snapshot with a per-video collectedAt, not a channel-level history. The format-diversity half is computable (signature entropy, pooled spearman vs median views = +0.01) but with no growth outcome to correlate it against.

Caveat: Do not substitute median views for growth rate here — the claim is explicitly about trajectory after a diversity choice, and a cross-sectional view comparison would confound channel age, niche and subscriber base.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply at different channel sizes. The question that separates them:

Is the channel already being SERVED impressions it is failing to convert, or is it not being served at all? Retention work can only compound if distribution already exists to be amplified — Joos's channel was at 17M monthly views when he started, i.e. YouTube was already handing it audience. The audits' channels are at 54k-988k median first-28d views, where the gap is upstream. Our own data settles the video-level half of this: rank correlation between retention-at-50% and first-28d views is NEGATIVE on five of six channels (Channel C -0.45, Channel D -0.51, Channel E -0.85, Channel A -0.47, Channel F -0.89; Channel G 0.07). Within a channel, the videos that reached furthest retained WORSE — because reach recruits non-core viewers who leave earlier. So 'improve retention' is not a lever on views at the video level; it is at best a channel-level lever operating through a distribution regime our data does not cover. The discriminating question is the traffic-source mix, which we do not hold.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does the 'experiment' vary an INPUT inside the preserved viewer contract, or vary the contract itself? The ideation packet already supplies the discipline (8ab1156f2655: the second episode of a candidate format preserves the structure and changes exactly one major input). Joos's experimental slot is coherent only if the promised transformation is held constant and the topic, cast, constraint or setting is what moves; Chaudry's punished video is one where the transformation itself changed. So the missing context is: what does this audience's return depend on — the WORLD (creator, cast, recurring frame, where a new topic is welcome) or the TRANSFORMATION (a specific outcome they came for, where a new topic reads as a bait-and-switch)? Ask which of the two the channel's top comments are about.

Earlier one-off check

Predates the measurement ledger — a single manual pass, not a repeated test. With nothing measured yet, this check is the only evidence behind the standing above.

Checked: Both stores are recency-windowed: the channel knowledge bases hold the most recent 9-30 videos, and the niche corpus holds ~10-40 recent uploads per channel (1,290 videos over 46 channels). No channel's first upload is in the data, so no upload index can be computed for any breakout.

Caveat: This is a fixable gap — a full uploads-playlist crawl would give upload indices cheaply — but it would still face survivorship bias, since only channels that broke out are visible for the count. The honest version of the test needs channels that never broke out as the denominator.

we always hear about these people who blow up. First video you blow up, second video you blow up. Whatever. A lot of people actually require 50, 60, 70 videos in order to blow up. It's unfortunate, but that's just how it is, because it takes that long to discover a good audience.
Theory strategy
Making a video 'additive' — teaching or inspiring something beyond entertainment — increases performance via sharing, not via retention alone.
Source: CreatorNow

Source: idea-engine research dossier
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Does this footage support SIX DISTINCT PROMISES, or one promise cut into six pieces? Khare is right about PARTS — a part-two inherits a weakened package and asks the viewer to have seen part one. The packet's six are not parts: 'packing' and 'campsite ranking' are separate questions with separate titles, separate thumbnails and partly separate audiences, and none of them requires the others. So the rule is not about count at all, it is about whether each upload has an independent, clickable promise that stands alone. The store also supplies the failure mode at the other extreme: Channel I's c112e6452da9 — 30 daily uploads bought a subscriber bump then flatlined by day 30 as reach fell back to the core (~125k average down to 30-40k), which is what happens when the pieces have no independent promise. our strategist's 5e3bd00115b5 (2-4 long-form from a month-long trip) sits between the two and is the operating compromise.

Theory production · Maker / build

Source: our own channel audits
Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is the imperfection in the SUBJECT or in the CRAFT? A cut that fails, a measurement that is wrong, a joint that has to be redone is evidence that the process shown is real — it is content, and it is what makes the viewer feel they are building alongside. Clipped audio, a soft focus pull, an unbalanced grade, a jump cut that loses the thread is evidence that the MAKER is careless, and the viewer transfers that judgement to the information. The repaired rule: never hide the subject's failures, never show the craft's. This also disarms Galloway's 21cb7a502c05 ('production upgrades do not make outliers') — polish is a floor condition for trust in an information niche, not a lever on reach.

Reconciled with a conflicting claim

Another claim in this base says something incompatible, and it is not a contradiction — the two apply to different kinds of channel. The question that separates them:

Is this an EPISODE or a TENTPOLE? Hurwitz's 5cb5e965b040 already draws the line: regular uploads are episodes of an open-ended series, tentpoles are finite films, and the two require different structures. An episodic container has slack — the metric can legitimately set the dial because the format can absorb another segment. A tentpole's length is determined by its payoff, and cutting to hit a number breaks the thing people came for. Our own data supports the audits' direction within episodic catalogues: the longer half of the catalogue won on median first-28d views for six of seven channels (Channel C 321,662 vs 291,465; Channel D 65,205 vs 48,143; Channel A 251,961 vs 218,645; Channel F 1,012,676 vs 963,861; Channel B 287,063 vs 207,873; Channel G 485,039 vs 367,785). The single exception is Channel E — the channel with by far the longest median duration at 52 minutes — where longer LOST (691,316 vs 863,878). That is the shape of a permission-to-lengthen rule with a channel-specific ceiling, not a universal one, and it is why the rule must be re-read each quarter rather than applied once.
